projects.title: Amaze.me
projects.summary: A two-dimensional maze generator and three-dimensional visualiser for the web.

body.text: A web app that generates random mazes and visualises them in 3D, written in TypeScript with Three.js for rendering and Joy UI for its interface.

projects.title: Audio-visual data processing
projects.summary: A collection of assignments for the audio-visual data processing course at ENSEEIHT, with compiled reports.

body.text: Assignments for the audio-visual data processing course at ENSEEIHT. The compiled reports are published online.

projects.title: Avatar
projects.summary: A web-based SVG avatar generator that recolours a profile picture from a chosen palette.

body.text: A web tool for creating variations of one specific profile picture by changing its colour palette. It does not alter the avatar's design or structure.

projects.title: Carbon Atlas
projects.summary: An interactive dashboard that visualises carbon projects on a world map, with filterable project cards, animated links between markers and cards, a command palette and a KPI overview.

meta.label: Stack
meta.value: React, TypeScript, Vite, MUI Joy, Mapbox GL, Motion, Recharts

body.text: An interactive dashboard for visualising carbon projects on a world map with detailed project information: an interactive map with project markers, a sidebar of filterable project cards, animated lines connecting markers to cards, a command palette for quick navigation and a KPI overview.
It is a fork of Kanop's 2026 user interface capabilities demo, published here with the explicit authorisation of the company.

projects.title: CLIfford
projects.summary: A simple and highly customisable command line interface for C++ applications.

body.text: A generic command line interface for C++ applications, with custom commands, arguments and options, an integrated help system and splash screen, and colour support.

projects.title: Cron
projects.summary: An Android alarm app that picks your wake time from your calendar, location, travel time and sleep signals.

body.text: An Android smart alarm that decides each evening when to wake you, from your calendar, your location, the travel time to your first commitment and overnight sleep signals. A second, fixed alarm is armed as a safety floor. The evening plan is computed with Anthropic's Claude.

projects.title: Epidemic spreading
projects.summary: A graph theory study of the propagation of an epidemic, written as a Julia notebook.

body.text: A graph theory study about the propagation of an epidemic, in a notebook meant to be run with the Julia Jupyter kernel.

projects.title: ESP string lights
projects.summary: An MQTT-enabled controller for string lights with several effects, designed for the ESP32.

body.text: An MQTT-enabled controller for string lights with multiple effects and a physical button, designed for the ESP32, compatible with Home Assistant, and keeping its state across power cycles.

projects.title: Hull breach tracking
projects.summary: A physics engine that simulates breaches in a ship's hull and detects their location through mechanical wave analysis.

body.text: A dynamic physics engine which simulates breaches in a ship's hull, and the many ways of detecting them and finding their location through mechanical wave analysis.
It was meant to be completed by June 2020 as part of the French TIPE oral exams; the exams were cancelled because of the COVID crisis.

projects.title: Hypergon
projects.summary: A proof of concept for a 4D rendering engine in C++.

body.text: A proof of concept for a 4D rendering engine, built with OpenGL, GLFW and GLM. A separate repository is a template for applications built on it.

projects.title: IPvChat
projects.summary: A C++ chat client and server infrastructure for Linux, configured with CMake.

body.text: A chat client-server infrastructure written in C++, split into a client and a server, both configured with CMake and built for Linux.

projects.title: ISF design system
projects.summary: A first draft of the design system of Ingénieurs sans frontières (ISF).

body.text: A first draft of the design system of Ingénieurs sans frontières (ISF), built with Next.js.

projects.title: Lidar
projects.summary: A virtual reality game about escaping a maze you cannot see, using a lidar to scan your surroundings.

body.text: A virtual reality game where you have to find your way out of a maze you cannot see: you use your lidar, a laser coupled with a light sensor, to scan your surroundings and avoid obstacles.
It is inspired by the Garry's Mod addon LIDAR by datæ, and is still in early development: playable, with many features missing.

projects.title: Light engine
projects.summary: An inverse rasterizer engine demo in Java and Swing, extended with camera movement and a better interface.

body.text: An inverse rasterizer engine demo, written in Java using Swing. Most calculations run on the CPU, which limits performance, but it is a sample implementation of the rasterization process.
It is a heavily modified version of a rasterizer by C. Dehais, S. Mondet and G. Morin, with camera movement, further optimisation and a better interface.

projects.title: Linda
projects.summary: A remotely accessible, thread-safe tuple database implemented in Java with RMI remote objects.

body.text: A remotely accessible Tuple database, implemented in Java using RMI remote objects. Mostly a proof of concept.

projects.title: Material sticky header
projects.summary: A proof of concept of Android's scroll-snap settings header behaviour in React and TypeScript.

body.text: A proof of concept implementation of Android's scroll-snap settings header: a sticky header that transitions between states with the scroll position, mimicking the native Android settings screen.

projects.title: Moneytor
projects.summary: A lightweight web app that visualises your coding activity from the Wakatime API and calculates your earnings from your hourly rate.

body.text: A lightweight web application built on the Wakatime API. It shows your coding activity in a simple way and calculates earnings from your hourly rate. It needs a Wakatime API key.

projects.title: Joy UI palette generator
projects.summary: A procedural, accessible palette generator for the MUI Joy library, working in the OKLCH colour space.

body.text: Generates accessible colour palettes for Joy UI in OKLCH, with gamut mapping to sRGB, WCAG 2.1 and APCA contrast validation, all five semantic palettes, and exports to TypeScript, CSS variables, JSON and Tailwind.

projects.title: Pconsole
projects.summary: A tiny, easy-to-use runtime console for Panda3D-powered applications, published on PyPI.

body.text: A tiny runtime console for Panda3D applications. You give it a dictionary of command names and functions, a key to toggle it, and a command line is available in your running app. It is installable with pip install pconsole.

projects.title: Catalyst
projects.summary: Catalyst is the code name of this website: a personal archive organised around places, with an interactive pixel-art globe that hands over to a street map.

meta.label: Stack
meta.value: React Router, TypeScript, Three.js, MapLibre, Hono

body.text: Catalyst is the project name of this website. It is a personal archive organised around places: an interactive globe is the main way to discover curated places and the stories, projects, articles and artworks attached to them, and it hands over to a street map when you zoom in.

The site is a monorepo with a server-rendered web app, a read-only public API and a published content projection. The content itself lives in a separate private repository and reaches the public one only as a reviewed pull request. The first version, from 2022, was an e-portfolio built with React, React Spring and MUI Joy.

projects.title: PyOS
projects.summary: An orbital mechanics simulator written entirely in Python on the Panda3D engine. PyOS stands for Python orbit simulator.

body.text: PyOS is an orbital mechanics simulator, written entirely in Python on top of the Panda3D engine.

It was created for a computer science class at PCSI Déodat de Séverac in Toulouse, and was heavily inspired by Universe Sandbox, a game by Giant Army. It was meant to become a sandbox space game and is now archived.

projects.title: Randomite
projects.summary: A pseudo-random number generator and visualiser for the web, with a gaussian generator and charts.

body.text: A web app that generates pseudo-random numbers and visualises them in several ways, with the ECharts library and Joy UI.

projects.title: Raycast capture and create
projects.summary: A Raycast extension that turns a selected region of your screen into a Google Task or a macOS Calendar event.

body.text: A Raycast extension with two commands: select any region of your screen and it becomes a Google Task (with an inferred title, note and due date) or a macOS Calendar event. The screenshot is interpreted with Claude Vision.

projects.title: Slashboard
projects.summary: A dashboard to monitor the activity and performance of your home servers: an Electron and React desktop client, and a lightweight Node.js agent (Pulsar) on each server.

body.text: A simple and convenient way to monitor the activity and performance of your servers: a desktop client built with Electron and React, which talks to Slashboard Pulsar, a lightweight Node.js app installed on each server.

projects.title: Spectrum visualizer
projects.summary: A demo of a custom spectrum visualisation component for microphone recording interfaces.

body.text: A demo application of a custom spectrum visualisation component: real-time audio visualisation from the microphone, with customisable colour schemes and a responsive layout.

projects.title: Spinel
projects.summary: An OpenGL-based 3D rendering engine written in Java, created as part of the 7map project.

body.text: Spinel is an OpenGL-based 3D rendering engine, written in Java and created as part of the 7map project.

projects.title: SVG gradients
projects.summary: A collection of experiments with grainy, noisy SVG gradients built on turbulence filters.

body.text: Experiments with SVG turbulence-based gradients. A LinearGradient component is a drop-in replacement for the standard SVG linearGradient element, documented in the source with examples.

projects.title: Terrain interpolation
projects.summary: An OpenGL proof of concept of a procedural terrain interpolation algorithm, documented in French.

body.text: A proof of concept for terrain interpolation, built with OpenGL, GLFW and GLM. The documentation is in French and most comments are in English.

projects.title: Voxelife
projects.summary: A three-dimensional Conway's Game of Life in C++ and OpenGL.

body.text: A proof of concept of a three-dimensional game of life simulation, written in C++ with OpenGL for rendering.

projects.title: Vshell
projects.summary: A very basic Unix shell written in C as a proof of concept.

body.text: A basic shell in C with job control (fg, bg, stop, jobs, exit), pipes and background jobs.

projects.title: Wave engine
projects.summary: A wave-motion particle simulator in Python, powered by Panda3D.

body.text: A wave-motion particle simulator written in Python and rendered with Panda3D. The physical constants (rigidity, time scale, friction) are variables at the top of the code.

projects.title: Window controls overlay demo
projects.summary: A demo of the Window Controls Overlay API in an installable web app, for collapsing navigation bars into the title bar.

body.text: An experiment with the Window Controls Overlay API in a progressive web app, which lets a desktop PWA use the title bar area for its own navigation.

projects.title: WhatsApp content moderation
projects.summary: A background-hosted "digital curtain" for a personal WhatsApp account: it links as a companion device, runs messages from chosen contacts through a local LLM classifier, deletes flagged ones locally and warns or temporarily blocks after repeated strikes.

body.text: A localised, background-hosted "digital curtain" for a personal WhatsApp account. It links to the account as a headless companion device, runs incoming messages from an operator-chosen set of monitored contacts through an LLM classifier, deletes flagged messages locally ("delete for me"), sends a warning, and temporarily blocks a contact after repeated strikes. Repeated unanswered calls are handled the same way.
A web control app shows the moderated contacts, an activity log, the settings and the policy. It is pre-release: it ships with a shadow mode that only logs, and a live demo with invented data.

articles.title: Rendering techniques applied to caustics
articles.summary: A review of the techniques used to render caustics: texture projections, ray tracing, volumetric lighting, and real-time simulation as opposed to precomputed rendering.

body.text: Elliot Négrel-Jerzy, ENSEEIHT - Computer Science Dept.
Abstract

Replicating reality is a goal that we have essentially always been striving to achieve. This obsession with realism started with cave paintings, and has now reached the age of computer-generated imagery, with highly advanced, mathematically-proven methods, one of these being caustics. The existing literature does cover many approaches to this phenomenon, and their perks, including the following, which we intend to discuss here: we’ll explore texture projections, ray-tracing, volumetric lighting, and real-time simulation, opposed to precomputed rendering. Despite the variety of these subjects, this paper’s fundamental aim is to explain in simple words the idea behind these methods, as well as what makes them so effective.
Cost-performance trade-off

The most obvious distinction which comes to mind when talking about rendering objects, is between real-time and precomputed simulations. Both approaches do obviously offer unique advantages which are sought after in specific fields of computer imagery.

Pre-rendering, as expected, is not suitable for videogames, or any kind of interactive medium, since it consists of generating the images/video feed beforehand. This is done very often on a powerful machine, allowing for more complex and detailed simulations, while keeping the rendering speeds pretty low compared to what it would take for an average computer to do the same. Therefore, this technique is mostly used in cinematography and filmmaking, with software such as Blender 3D (open source), Cinema 4D, 3ds Max and many others (Fig. 1).
Fig. 1: Most popular 3D Modelling tools in 2016, sorted by market presence vertically and user satisfaction horizontally (G2, 2016)

In contrast, real-time rendering techniques are extensively becoming the preferred method for 3D imagery (Christen, 2017), due to their speed, which allows for an efficient workflow, and a quick visualisation of the final result. Now, obviously, this speed doesn’t come without a cost: accuracy is considered low priority, hence algorithms which require heavy computations will often be replaced with visually similar, although physically incorrect alternatives.

However, it is important to note that nowadays, the frontier between these two categories is becoming thinner with the constant increase in computing power, and the new algorithms made available on the market (cf. Unreal Engine 5 – Lumen Global Illumination and Reflections). On the same note, software usually used in pre-computed rendering can be applied to virtual reality, and other forms of interactive 3D visualization in some very specific hardware configurations (Interactive rendering with blender cycles for virtual reality using hpc clusters, 2019), such as the one described below (Fig. 2). Here, the computing power is fully relocated to a high-performance computing data centre, which can handle the rendering of 60 images in one second. This cloud-computing infrastructure receives lightweight network packets containing user input data, and sends back compressed images back to the user’s interface.
Fig. 2: Cloud-computing infrastructure, featuring an HPC distributed rendering Cluster (Interactive rendering with blender cycles for virtual reality using hpc clusters, 2019)
Caustic Rendering

Now that we have properly defined the technical solutions used in the field of computer-generated imagery, we can finally explore in detail what Caustics are, and how most render engines approach them.

Caustic networks are shapes of concentrated light projected onto a surface, which are created when rays of light pass through a curved object made of a transparent material. A common occurrence of these optic artefacts is a glass of water exposed to a powerful light source (Fig. 3). Again, various methods are available. The most naïve approach uses ray-tracing (Wyman, et al., 2004) to calculate the colour of each pixel of the image. To keep things simple, it can be summarized in the following manner: the computer casts a ray from each pixel of the camera, which intersects both the pixel of the near plane¹ (see Fig. 4) and the eye point (centre of the projection). This ray then bounces off the faces of the objects it encounters, or gets through them, following the basic principles of refraction and reflection angles; throughout this process, it gains or loses energy, as the surfaces it hits absorb part of it. The ray will keep on bouncing until a maximum number of iterations (set by the user) is reached. If by then it has not collided with a light source, the pixel will be black, or else it will inherit the light source’s colour (this is a clear oversimplification of the process, if you want to know more about it, please check the bibliography (Arvo, 1986)).

¹ The near plane, or near clipping plane lies perpendicular to the camera direction. The distance from the camera (eye point) to the near plane is the closest distance that any object can be to the camera while still remaining in the view.
Fig. 3: Caustics created by a glass of water (cgiknowledge, 2013)
Fig. 4: Common representation of a virtual camera in 3D rendering (Moccozet, 2008)

This approach is efficient, but as you might have guessed by now, extremely costly and slow. Hence, the preferred technique in the video game and virtual/augmented reality industry, attempts to replace most of these heavy calculations with pre-computed models (Zeltner, et al., 2020), at the expense of accuracy. This sacrifice is however absolutely legitimate, since as long as the player does not physically interact with the shape of the object through which light shines, there is no reason for the game to recompute the aforementioned model in real-time.

A common example (Dual Heights Software AB, 2021) of its use is water: pre-calculated caustics textures are projected onto the ocean/pool floor (Fig. 5) and distorted to create the illusion of movement, while the water surface itself is displaced according to an independent noise texture. The lack of consistency between cause (distortion of the water surface) and effect (resulting caustic network) remains unnoticed as long as the waves are low in height and uniform.
Fig. 5: Caustic network textures projected onto various shapes in Unity 3D (Dual Heights Software AB, 2021)

More complex situations, such as moving glass surfaces or dynamic bodies of water, require more advanced models (Villani, 2009), which allow the algorithm to avoid using actual ray-tracing, and still get significantly convincing results.
Conclusion

With the increasing presence of virtual and augmented reality in our lives on a daily basis, computer graphics have become a major part of our lives, and before we know it, we might as well end up spending more time in simulated environments than in our actual world. Thus, the breakthroughs made in the field of lighting, and more specifically caustics are more than necessary, they are vital to our mental health in the long run. Despite the fact that at this point, we still need to use smart tricks (Xiao, et al., 2020) to get away with the extensive complexity and cost of our algorithms, it is safe to assume that, in a couple years, we’ll have sorted these issues out, either by improving our hardware or by creating new, more efficient software solutions.
References

articles.title: Virtual reality technologies
articles.summary: A comparison of the hardware, tracking systems and software behind virtual reality headsets, summarising the available literature.

body.text: Elliot Négrel-Jerzy, ENSEEIHT - Computer Science Dept.
Abstract

Virtual reality, a dream become reality, a software marvel combined with decades of experience in computer hardware, sensors, but also, most importantly a tool, now used in a large variety of domains. Although at first sight, the concept might seem easy to get a grasp of, the technology behind it is considerably more complex than one might think at first sight. The available literature is extremely detailed and comprehensive; therefore, this article’s aim is to compare and summarize in a clear and concise manner the many approaches chosen to address the subject. We’ll be exploring the existing hardware, as well as the most commonly used tracking systems and the software bringing this whole machinery to life.
VR display hardware solutions

The state-of-the-art virtual reality headsets available on the market have led major companies such as Meta or Google to seriously consider investing in this domain, despite the initial drawbacks that the new technology came with. Their interest is, to this day, one of the main reasons why these devices are being mass produced, and are as a result, substantially cheap.

After taking a look at the actual design of one of these headsets (Parkin, 2014), we can identify three “main” components, the first being the circuit board. It features a highly powerful graphical processing unit, due to the very high requirements in terms of display latency: extended looking at a slow and unresponsive video feed has proven to induce nausea and headaches.
Figure 1: Inside view of an Oculus Rift VR headset (Parkin, 2014)

This board is then connected to a high-definition display module, whose technology can vary depending on the budget (LCD or OLED solutions are often preferred). However, the most commonly encountered design uses a backlit liquid crystal display, i.e., a non-emissive, translucent layer of so-called liquid crystals (extensively small cells whose color can be dynamically changed by applying a specific voltage for each color), coupled with a monochrome light-emitting backlight unit (BLU), which ensured the visibility of the content displayed on the aforementioned layer, by shining light through it.
Figure 2: Schematic diagram of an LCD (Liquid crystal display and organic light-emitting diode display: present status and future perspectives, 2017)

Finally, two lenses are positioned in front of both eyes, ensuring that the perceived image is positioned “at infinity”, so as to reduce eye strain. This setting essentially means that the light coming from the objects as seen through the lens will appear to be coming from a very long distance, thus allowing the user’s eyes to effortlessly focus on them.
At this point, we do have a fairly accurate view of how an average entry-level VR headset’s works; therefore, we can dive into the existing hardware solutions used in movement and position tracking.
Tracking systems

Presently, virtual reality is being used in a plethora of domains, most of which require an interaction between the user and the virtual environment in which he is immersed, hence the necessity of tracking movement and position in space, sometimes even to the accuracy level of finger movement.

Multiple solutions do exist, and yet it would be a lie to say that these are in competition on the market, as each and every single one of them is more suitable for certain specific use cases. Open environments with great freedom of movement, such as virtual reality battle arenas (e.g., EVA) or military combat training infrastructure (Lele, 2011), will require positional tracking of limbs and weapons, which best works using optical tracking methods. The monitored zone cannot be infinite, and must be surrounded with cameras, coupled with highly powerful light projectors (preferably infrared, due to its imperceptibility to the human eye). The user should be equipped with judiciously placed retro-reflective markers, so as to minimize the positional estimation error; obviously, these markers are in general specifically designed to reflect extremely well the light frequency emitted by the aforementioned projectors. In the end, what the cameras see is an extremely dark image, covered with blindingly white dots, which correspond to the limbs of the user, and whose coordinates can later be determined, in order to programmatically calculate his position. Variations of this method may involve laser emitters instead of markers (Simulation of a virtual reality tracking system, 2011), whose beams will project dots of light on the walls of the monitored room. However, both techniques make use of cameras when it comes to locating them.
Figure 3: Visualization of an optical tracker's detection system (RetroTracker: Upgrading Existing Virtual Reality Tracking Systems, 2019)

High precision motion capture is usually sought after in VR apps which call for (included but not limited to) hand-gesture detection and close contact interactions with the environment. Again, several solutions are available to the public: optical detection in conjunction with AI algorithms, or gloves/suits equipped with structural deformation sensors.
Figure 4: Motion capture using an Optitrack marker suit and IMU-based gloves (Parger, et al., 2020)
Yet, these systems could never be this efficient if it wasn’t for the software that analyses the generated data.
Software appliances

The main challenge that programmers have to face when designing so-called “VR-ready” software, is the need for two points of view, or cameras, one for each eye. This is due to the fact that our perception of depth is highly dependent on our ability to merge two slightly different images, allowing us to see both sides of an object at the same time when it is close to us.

The drastically different interface, when comparing a headset to a common computer monitor also requires many modifications in terms of user interface, but also of sound quality and graphics. Rendering techniques such as caustic shading (Négrel-Jerzy, 2022) or ray tracing may be implemented with the aim to improve the realism of an environment in which the user is supposed to feel immersed.
Conclusion

The emergence of fully virtual worlds such as the metaverse by Meta (formerly Facebook) shows the increasing importance of VR in our lives, sometimes without the need for special gear: augmented reality is slowly making its way into our daily routines, mostly through some of our smartphone applications. This technology is constantly evolving, breakthroughs are being made every day, improving both its looks and its performance. And yet, this persistent seeking of innovation and progress has been proven to be our society’s main vulnerability. With climate change on our doorstep, should we really keep on following such an ethically unacceptable industrial model? It is to be hopped that we will eventually learn from our mistakes, and save ourselves from the consequences of our own choices.

poems.title: Crépuscule grec
poems.summary: Un poème sur un village et ses collines, à midi, vu depuis un banc.

stanzas: Ce matin les toits brillent,
inondés de soleil.
Sur les coteaux vermeils
des enfants s'éparpillent.
Couronnant le village telle une mitre grise,
des massifs rocheux dominent l'horizon.
Et du haut de leurs cimes embrumées, le gazon
déverse sa verdure sur un clocher d'église.
Depuis un banc, assis, je contemple la vue.
Je savoure ce calme solennel que parfois
ponctuent les tons joyeux de ses rires, de sa voix.
Les yeux rivés sur ce spectacle imprévu,
je caresse sa main. Mes démons se sont tus,
comme attendris peut-être, par la splendeur profonde
de ce moment de paix et d'amour impromptu.
Il est bientôt midi, la lumière furibonde
donne à ses traits marbrés des reflets de statue.

poems.title: Forêt dansante
poems.summary: Un quatrain sur un acrobate sous les chênes.

stanzas: Lourde est la corde et brave est l'habile acrobate
sous les chênes d'argent, il s'élance, gracieux
du feuillage rayonne un soleil écarlate
seuls témoins de l'exploit, s'émerveillent les cieux

poems.title: L'exil
poems.summary: Un poème sur une ville endeuillée et le départ qui approche.

stanzas: Ce soir la ville est morne, les arbres sont en deuil.
Les carreaux larmoyants ont des teintes bleuâtres.
Pourtant, aucun passant ne pleure, aucun cercueil
dans les rues désertées d'un Paris acariâtre.
Ce teint sombre et muet, ce silence morose,
il trouve son ardeur dans mon esprit hagard.
Pour l'apaiser, tantôt j'ai couché ci ma prose
mais elle ne peut défaire mes chaînes. Je m'égare
dans les traits dilués par les larmes versées.
Bientôt je partirai, et mes rêves d'enfants
resteront tous ici. Et c'est le cœur gercé
que je m'assoupirai à l'aube, caressant
d'une main frémissante, le velours des fauteuils.
Un son strident retentira, note angoissante,
glas sourd annonçant mon exil; en un clin d'œil
les balustrades, les toitures grises opalescentes
seront déjà perdues dans la brume aurorale.

poems.title: Le comédien
poems.summary: Un poème sur un comédien d'improvisation qui affronte un cavalier surgi de la brume.

stanzas: Sur la scène embrumée d'illusions impalpables
se dresse un comédien, emblème du chaos.
De son esprit radieux, ruissellent quelques fables
mais nul ne voit vraiment, de fin à son propos.
C'est néanmoins sans but, étourdi formidable,
qu'il déclame fièrement sa tirade, et là-haut
sa muse, divertie, cache d'un air affable
la clé tant convoitée du trésor qu'est l'impro.
Mais voilà que des brumes indéfinies, macabres
se dessine soudain, l'ombre d'un cavalier
sa monture invisible, frémit, hennit, se cabre
et lacère le brouillard de ses sabots d'acier.
Le comédien frissonne, mais se pare au combat
des éclairs jaillissent de ses mains argentées.
Le premier coup est sien, et de ses feux l'éclat
n'a d'égal ici bas que sa dextérité.

poems.title: Les pèlerins du rail
poems.summary: Un poème sur un trajet en train à Paris, du soir à la nuit.

stanzas: La ville est assoupie, le soleil est de glace
Des reflets palpitants sur les vitres du train
s'élèvent des figures, sombres, et c'est l'audace
de l'habile architecte, artiste dont l'entrain
a su mouvoir des villes, fédérer des génies
qui défie, souveraine, l'horizon monotone
d'un Paris dont Montmartre est le seul insoumis.
Le ciel est de rubis, comme en un soir d'automne.
Nuit d'été, chaleur sourde, aux couleurs estompées
Lueurs mourantes et mornes, baignant de leurs pénombre
le satin suranné des rideaux déchirés
Ronflement monotone, murmure perdu dans l'ombre
des passagers bercés par la voie délabrée.

poems.title: Ode au désert
poems.summary: Une ode à un chemin de terre et au désert, au crépuscule.

stanzas: Sur ce chemin terreux perdu dans le lointain,
à travers des torrents et des falaises antiques,
l'herbe courbe l'échine, et les vents incertains
caressent la dentelle infinie et lithique
des berges désolées de ce désert brumeux.
Parmi les roches ocres, nul être ne subsiste,
et seul le sable blanc, aux reflets résineux,
tourbillonne en silence, et recouvre la piste.
La route est longue, hélas ! Pourpre est le crépuscule.
Les phares scintillants du monstre de métal
peinent à révéler les arbres minuscules
cernant le précipice de sinistres pétales.

poems.title: Pénombre d'été
poems.summary: Un poème sur une chambre en pénombre, en été.

stanzas: Enseveli, rêveur, parmi les draps de nacre,
il observe ahuri, arborant un sourire,
son reflet translucide dans le miroir de cire
aux teintes grisonnantes, emplies de senteurs âcres.
Des stores bancals au bois fendu, irrégulier,
se déverse un soleil hésitant et fugace.
Il répand sur les murs sa chevelure de glace
et strie de son chaos la pièce immaculée.
Rayonnante de joie, le visage radiant,
elle se dresse dans l'ombre telle une idole antique
et s'esclaffe d'un rire aux timbres idylliques,
admirant, inlassable, son accomplissement.

poems.title: Prose nocturne
poems.summary: Un poème en prose sur une pièce éclairée de néons bleus.

stanzas: Dans la pénombre jaunâtre et bleutée
d'un bouge obscur aux meubles clairsemés,
des néons bleus bourdonnent tristement.
Une lueur sombre mais grésillante
baigne les murs de tons froids, ambigus.
Et dans un coin se blottit, assoupi,
un être pâle à la chevelure noire.
Sur son visage creusé par l'insomnie
se réverbèrent des sigles mystérieux.
Des ombres sourdes, quelques notes
chétives et faibles et cependant dansantes,
seule trace d'un monde proche de l’irréel.
Les vers s'effondrent, tels les piliers centenaires d'un édifice ancien,
et l'esprit se fragmente, dans un cri déchirant plein de frayeur et d'angoisse.

poems.title: Sinking
poems.summary: A short poem about melancholy as a slow drowning.

stanzas: Melancholy kicking in, like waves splashing on a rundown pier
Surges of pain flashing up your spine, exploding in your head
washing up the remains of your mind, dragging you down the well
like a sinking boat, you fight for your life, for the air, for the freedom
but you don't even know what it feels like anymore.
Your face fades away in the dark, oily water, and your mouth
opens and close again and again, in a futile survival instinct.

poems.title: The enslaved acrobat
poems.summary: A poem in four quatrains about a prisoner acrobat on a battlefield at night.

stanzas: Rundown gears rumble in the night,
weeping engines covered in tears and dust.
The prisoner rushes into the fight,
his mind is weak and overcome with rust.
The ground is harsh and unforgiving;
under the sand, lie the defeated,
their daggers raised below, their king
perished at their side, beheaded.
Yet the prisoner's feet fly above
like a ghostly bird, he hovers
upon the moonlit pond where love's
only presence is scattered clovers.
The field is cold, the moon is bright
a drop of blood has stained the moss.
Another life is claimed tonight
the prisoner has joined the lost.

poems.title: The traveler
poems.summary: A four-line poem about being lost in a foreign town at night.

stanzas: Lost in a town whose mirror lake shines bright
Arcane slang that I can't comprehend
I tirelessly seek at night
A magic place where heaven knows no end.
